stem.text: A function f has derivative \( f'(x) = -\frac{3\left(x + 4\right)\left(x - 4\right)}{\left(x - 2\right)^{2}} \) for all \( x \ne 2 \), where f is not defined at \( x = 2 \). On what open intervals is f increasing? Give a reason for the answer.

answer_key.label: f is increasing on the intervals \( (-4, 2) \) and \( (2, 4) \), because \( f'(x) > 0 \) on each of those intervals.

worked_solution.text: The sign of f' can change only where \( f'(x) = 0 \) at \( x = -4 \) and \( x = 4 \), and f' is undefined at \( x = 2 \), which is not in the domain of f.
worked_solution.rule_named: partition points of the sign chart

worked_solution.text: Testing one point in each piece gives \( f'(x) > 0 \) on the intervals \( (-4, 2) \) and \( (2, 4) \) and \( f'(x) < 0 \) on the intervals \( (-\infty, -4) \) and \( (4, \infty) \).
So f is increasing on the intervals \( (-4, 2) \) and \( (2, 4) \), because \( f'(x) > 0 \) on each of those intervals.
worked_solution.rule_named: sign of the derivative gives the direction of the function

options.label: f is increasing on the intervals \( (-\infty, -4) \) and \( (4, \infty) \), because \( f'(x) > 0 \) on each of those intervals.
options.derivation: the sign of f' read backwards, so the pieces where f' has the opposite sign are reported

options.label: f is increasing on the interval \( (-4, 4) \), because \( f'(x) > 0 \) on that interval.
options.derivation: the two intervals on either side of the excluded point x = 2 joined into one interval across the gap

options.label: f is increasing on the intervals \( (-4, 2) \) and \( (2, 4) \), because it is positive there.
